title: The Evening Brief: Brigance's legacy, LIV's funding crisis, and a Scottish revolt at FIFA
dek: Evening brings the Ravens family's farewell to O.J. Brigance after a 19-year fight with ALS, while institutional turbulence deepens at LIV Golf and FIFA. College football adds stability with Michigan State's athletic director hire.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: O.J. Brigance died at 56 after surviving 19 years beyond his ALS prognosis, leaving behind a foundation and a changed culture in how the NFL supports players facing terminal illness. Meanwhile, LIV Golf faces unpaid vendor bills as Saudi funding ends this month, and FIFA's Infantino loses another confederation's backing as the 2027 presidential race takes shape.
bottom_line: O.J. Brigance's death closes a 19-year survival that far exceeded medical expectation and reshaped how the NFL approaches player mentorship during terminal illness. Institutional turbulence deepened elsewhere: LIV Golf faces unpaid vendor bills as Saudi funding ends this month and pursues BC Partners capital, while FIFA's Infantino lost the Scottish Football Association's support ahead of 2027's presidential election and faces a formal eligibility challenge. Watch for BC Partners to announce a funding commitment, FIFA's governance committee response to the ineligibility petition, and whether other confederations join Scotland's withdrawal from Infantino's re-election bid.
body: The evening's dominant story is the death of O.J. Brigance, the Baltimore Ravens' longtime player engagement adviser and Super Bowl XXXV champion linebacker, who died August 17 at 56 after a 19-year battle with ALS. Diagnosed in 2007 at age 37 with a prognosis of two to five years, Brigance outlived that estimate by more than a decade and a half. He recorded the Ravens' first tackle in their Super Bowl victory over the Giants in January 2001 and holds the singular distinction of winning both a Super Bowl and a Grey Cup for the same city, capturing the latter with the Baltimore Stallions in 1995. In his years as a Ravens adviser, Brigance became a central figure in the franchise's approach to player mentorship during hardship, founding the Brigance Brigade Foundation and reshaping how professional sports organizations support athletes facing terminal illness.

Monday's institutional news widens the ledger across the sports landscape. LIV Golf's financial position deteriorated further as vendors report unpaid invoices ranging from thousands to nearly $100,000, with minimal communication from the league's accounts receivable and legal departments. The Saudi Public Investment Fund's announced end to LIV funding at the close of 2026 means the crisis timing coincides with the calendar month: funding runs out this month. The league has filed a WARN Act notice signaling potential mass layoffs and is pursuing a funding commitment from BC Partners' credit division, but the vendor experience suggests operational strain is already visible. Meanwhile, the Scottish Football Association announced it will not vote for FIFA president Gianni Infantino in 2027, joining England, Wales, and the Republic of Ireland and aligning with UEFA's 55 member associations, which have threatened a boycott of all FIFA competitions. SFA chief executive Ian Maxwell cited governance failures and lack of transparency, stating that administrators should not be the focus after a World Cup and that something has gone wrong if off-the-field incidents overshadow on-the-field results. An advocacy group has also challenged Infantino's legal eligibility to run for a fourth term, introducing a governance dimension beyond electoral preference.

College sports brought one stabilizing move: Michigan State finalized a deal to hire Dan Bartholomae, the athletic director at Western Michigan since January 2022, to fill the leadership vacancy created by J Batt's departure to Kentucky. Bartholomae, 46, led Western Michigan to a men's hockey national title in 2025 and a MAC football championship while raising a record $21.8 million for the athletic department in 2025-26, signaling a focus on fundraising and program-building.

Into the final weeks of preseason and toward the regular season, injury reports accumulated in the NFL. Chicago Cubs shortstop Dansby Swanson has a Grade 2 oblique strain and is expected to miss four to six weeks after leaving Sunday's loss to St. Louis in the third inning due to left side discomfort. New Orleans Saints rookie wide receiver Jordyn Tyson suffered a right hamstring injury during a Thursday joint practice with Jacksonville and could miss approximately two months, potentially sidelining the No. 8 draft pick through at least Week 6 of the regular season.
